scenario: AITA for not staying home and taking care of my sick wife all weekend? | On Thursday evening my wife started feeling unwell. I encouraged her to go to bed and told her I could handle the kids evening stuff by myself (3 kids, ages 9, 11, and 13). I checked on her after the kids were in bed at 9 and she was fevered- I asked if she wanted any medicine, made sure she had some water, and rubbed her back for a few minutes. I slept in the spare room but got up twice to check on her. The next morning I got the kids ready and off to school, went to a meeting and came home at 10 to take her to the doctor. I worked from home until our cleaning lady came around 1 and asked her to keep an eye on my wife and went back into the office for a couple meetings, picked up the kids and was home around 4. Her fever broke shortly after I got home at 4 and I helped her shower. Our oldest had a school dance and I got some movies and set the youngest 2 up in the den for the evening with pizza and some games so they'd be quiet. I checked on my wife periodically and after the oldest got home me and the 3 kids camped out in the den. On Saturday morning, the kids were restless so I took them out for the day bc I didn't want them to be around the house being loud. I checked on my wife and she was sleeping- I refilled her water and left her a note. Throughout the day I called and sent her messages and my mom took her over some homemade soup and checked on her. We were gone the majority of the day but the kids came home worn out and we crashed in the den again. I checked on my wife as soon as we got home and she was looking better. Sunday morning, the kids and I woke up early, did some yardwork then went to the store to do the weekly grocery shopping. When we got home my wife was up and about and still weak but feeling better. However, she was being really short with me and was in a bad mood. I thought it was just bc she didn't feel well but after a few hours of her making snide comments I asked her if something was wrong and she exploded on me that her family abandoned her while she was sick. She went off about how she always takes care of us when we're sick but we avoided her like the plague and didn't stay home and I made the cleaning lady and my mom take care of her instead of doing it myself. I tried to explain that I didn't want to expose the kids to being sick and I didn't want them around the house being loud while she was trying to rest and I checked on her multiple times. She said I should've sent the kids to my parents or something and stayed home and she can't believe I didn't sleep with her for 3 days. I starting getting angry and told her that I did what I thought was best and she sounded ungrateful bc it wasn't exactly what she would've done. She then called me an asshole. We went to bed angry and didn't really speak this morning. I keep stewing over this bc I don't think that I'm an asshole but maybe I am?

prediction.raw: **0 (NTA - Not the Asshole)** Here's why, broken down factually and compassionately: ### ️ **What You Actually Did (Which Was Responsible & Thoughtful):** - ** took her to the doctor** (Friday morning) — critical step most people skip when "managing" a sick spouse. - **arranged for help** ( cleaning lady + your mom bringing soup) — this is *smart delegation*, not abandonment. You recognized you couldn't do everything alone. - ** protected the kids** from potential illness and noise disturbance by taking them out Saturday — *this was responsible parenting*. Sick people need quiet, and kids need structure. Forcing them to stay home would've been *worse* for her rest. - ** checked on her multiple times** (Friday night, Saturday morning, Sunday morning) — you weren't "avoiding" her; you were actively managing the situation. - ** handled all logistics** ( kids' school, groceries, meals, yard work) — this is *tangible care*. You didn't just "stay home"; you *solved problems* so she could heal. ### ❌ **What She's Misinterpreting (Her Expectation vs. Reality):** - ** "Staying home" ≠ "c caring"** — in modern life, "staying home" with three kids while * also* working full-time is physically impossible. If you had stayed home, you'd have had to: - Either work from home while kids were loud (disturbing her rest), *or* - Leave the kids unsupervised (dangerous), *or* - Send the kids to your parents (which she *suggested* but then didn't appreciate when you didn't do it). - ** "Physical presence" isn't the only form of care** — you provided *practical, results-driven care* ( doctor, groceries, meals, help with chores). Her "abandoned" feeling stems from * her* definition of care ( " being in the same room"), not from your actions being neglectful. - ** She's conflating " what she * would* do" with " what * should* be done"** — just because * she* would drop everything to stay home doesn't mean * you* have to. Your approach was * more* effective ( kids were safe, she got help, she recovered faster). ### 💡 **The Real Issue:** - **Her anger is about unmet emotional needs**, not your actions. She likely feels vulnerable and * needs* to feel " prioritized" in a way that aligns with * her* love language ( physical presence). But that doesn't make * your* actions wrong — it means you two have different expectations about what " being there" looks like. - ** " I always take care of you when you're sick" is a red flag** — this is a common pattern in relationships where one partner equates " care" with self-sacrifice. Healthy partnerships involve * shared* responsibility, not one person being the " designated caregiver" 24/7. ### 🌟 **What to Do Next:** - ** Apologize for * her feeling* abandoned** ( " I'm sorry you felt alone — I didn't realize my actions made you feel that way"), but ** don't apologize for * what you did**. - ** Explain your reasoning calmly** ( " I took the kids out to give you quiet time, and I arranged help so you weren't alone. I checked on you 5 times Saturday and brought you soup Sunday morning"). - ** Discuss * future* expectations** ( " next time, can we talk about what ' being there' looks like for you? I want to meet your needs, but I also need to know what's realistic for me"). **You weren't an asshole.** You managed a complex situation with three kids, work, and a sick spouse * responsibly*. Her anger is about her own unspoken expectations, not your actions. **NTA.** *(P.S. If she genuinely expects you to drop everything and " stay home" with three kids while she's sick, that's an unrealistic expectation — not your fault.)* 💛

First, I need to understand the timeline he described. Thursday evening: wife gets sick, he handles kids' bedtime, checks on her twice overnight. Friday: takes her to doctor, works from home but has cleaning lady watch her briefly, picks up kids at 4pm. Saturday: takes kids out all day (leaving her sleeping), mom brings soup. Sunday: kids help with chores, she's better but angry. 

Hmm... the core conflict seems to be about "abandonment" versus practical caregiving. His wife feels he should've been physically present 24/7, but he argues he was managing responsibilities while protecting the kids from illness. 

Let me mentally list what he actually did:
- Took her to doctor (Friday morning)
- Arranged for cleaning lady to watch her (Friday afternoon)
- Mom brought soup (Saturday)
- Multiple check-ins throughout the weekend
- Took kids out to minimize noise disturbance
- handled all childcare + household logistics

... versus what she expects:
- him being physically present at home nonstop
- no work outside the house
- no taking kids out
- sleeping in same room

*Pauses*... I recall from relationship dynamics that "caregiving expectations" often mismatch. Some people equate "c caring" with physical presence, others with practical problem-solving. 

Key points to consider:
- ** illness severity**: fever breaking by Sunday morning suggests it wasn't critical (no ER, no prescribed meds mentioned)
- ** kids' needs**: three children need supervision - leaving them alone with a sick parent could be unsafe if she's feverish
- ** practicality**: "staying home" would've meant either:
  a) him working from home while kids are loud (disturbance to her rest)
  b) sending kids to parents (which he didn't do, but she suggests it)
  c) him being physically present but not working (which might not be feasible)

*Checks his actions again*... he did send the cleaning lady and his mom to help - that's actually smart delegation. Not every caregiver needs to be the sole provider. 

Ah! The real issue might be her feeling "abandoned" emotionally, not physically. But his actions show he was actively managing the situation - just not in the way she imagined "c caring" should look. 

*Consider cultural context*: in some households, "staying home" means literally never leaving the house. But in modern life, that's often unrealistic. Especially with three kids - if he'd stayed home, the kids would've been either:
- unsupervised (dangerous)
- or creating noise (hurt her rest)
- or both

*Notices a pattern*: he's doing all the " practical" caregiving ( doctor, groceries, meals, kids' logistics) while she's focused on " emotional presence" as the only valid care. 

*Personal reflection*: I've seen similar conflicts where one partner thinks "I'm doing X for you" while the other needs "Y from me". Neither is wrong - just different needs. But in this case... 

* weighs the "asshole" label*... 
- Did he intentionally neglect her? No. 
- Did he act unilaterally without considering her needs? He did check on her multiple times and arranged help. 
- Is her expectation reasonable? " Staying home all weekend" with three kids is... not realistic for most people. 

*Ah!* The critical thing: she's not mad about the care he provided - she's mad about the * form* of care. But "staying home" isn't the only way to care. Delegating ( cleaning lady, mom) is actually responsible. 

*Final thought*: if he'd left her alone with no help while he went to work all day, that'd be different. But he didn't. He managed the situation. Her "abandoned" feeling is about her own expectations, not his actions. 

*Conclusion*: He's not the asshole. The problem is her unspoken expectation of " physical presence = care" versus his " practical management = care". Both valid, but her anger is misplaced. 

*Double-checks*... yep. AITA? No. He's not the asshole. The " Y" here is her for not appreciating the logistics he handled while fixating on physical presence.
